To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

sleep during euthermic arousals from hibernation in ground squirrels is affected by the duration of prior torpor, and that the effect can be described by an exponential function with a relatively short time constant.
sleep during euthermic recovery from torpor at an air temperature of 5°C is characterized by a high proportion of NREM sleep and by an increase in slow waves during the first part of euthermia.
sleep in hibernating ground squirrels is reduced during torpor, and that this reduction is proportional to the duration of prior torpor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of torpor on the sleep-wake cycle.
the function of sleep during arousal episodes in hibernating mammals.
the question how hibernation affects the sleep process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
torpor affects sleep in a way that the restorative function is inhibited.
torpor inhibiting the restorative function is not the only explanation of the observed changes in sleep structure during arousal episodes, but it is a major factor.
the sleep during arousal episodes in hibernating ground squirrels is affected both in intensity and structure by prior torpor duration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sleep in the hibernator European ground squirrel is a function of the prior duration of torpor, and that torpor affects sleep in a similar way to sleep deprivation in non-hibernators, i.e., torpor inhibits sleep's restorative function.
sleep is not restorative during hibernation.
torpor is not only a mechanism to reduce energy expenditure but also a mechanism to reduce the need to sleep.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of time an animal spends in torpor is an important factor to consider when interpreting EEG data recorded during arousal episodes in hibernators.
sleep during euthermia is affected by prior torpor duration, and this effect is most pronounced in the slow-wave frequency range.
sleep during euthermia following torpor is affected both in intensity and structure by prior torpor duration.
